title: The queue you're standing in is usually self-made.
subtitle: Arrival windows exist. Ignoring yours builds the line — and fills the confiscation bin.

text: Power strips, irons and travel kettles are commonly confiscated.
sub: Prohibited-item lists vary by line and by ship. Surge-protected strips and anything with a heating element are the usual seizures — read your own line's list before packing.

items.head: Arriving before your window
items.body: The terminal fills with people whose time has not come yet, and everybody waits longer for it.

items.head: Items that must be searched
items.body: A power strip in a carry-on means your bag is opened and gone through by hand.

items.head: Documents in the hold bag
items.body: The one case you cannot reach is the one the desk asks you to open.

items.head: Boarding at the popular hour
items.body: The middle of the window is the crowd. The edges of it are quiet.

title: What the terminal is actually doing

points.label: Arrival windows
points.value: Staggering guests is the only throughput mechanism a terminal really has.

points.label: Security screening
points.value: Every flagged bag becomes a hand search, and hand searches are slow.

points.label: Terminal capacity
points.value: Some ports are handling two or three ships across the same morning.

points.label: Manifest checks
points.value: Names, documents and forms are reconciled one guest at a time.

text: Embarkation has a harder deadline than any port call.
sub: Royal Caribbean, for instance, asks guests to be onboard no less than one hour before scheduled departure. Confirm the rule your own line applies.

text: Take your window, carry your documents, leave the power strip at home.
sub: That is most of it. The rest is arriving in the quieter half of your window and going straight up to lunch.

title: Send this to whoever packs the plugs
body: If it would help, I'll send back your line's prohibited-items page and your arrival window before you pack a single thing.
